result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.minimum_node_cut()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find minimum node cut between source and sink nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L20758-L20853){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.minimum_node_cut( source, sink, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns the set of nodes whose removal disconnects the source from the sink. Uses transformation to an edge connectivity problem where each node is split into in/out copies connected by unit capacity. The source and sink themselves are never included in the returned cut set. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node (integer ID or string label). [sink]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Sink node (integer ID or string label). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [set[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Set of node IDs forming the minimum node cut. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or sink node doesn't exist, or if they're the same. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The node connectivity between two nodes is the minimum number of nodes that must be removed to disconnect them. This is closely related to Menger's theorem. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this diamond-shaped graph, node `D` is the only bridge between the two paths connecting `A` to `E`, so it's the sole node in the minimum cut: ::: {#e6a5eca0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_edge("A", "B", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("A", "C", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("B", "D", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("C", "D", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("D", "E", auto_create_nodes=True) ) # Find nodes that separate A from E cut_nodes = graph.minimum_node_cut("A", "E") # Returns the ID of node D, the single point connecting both paths cut_nodes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {4} ``` ::: ::: The same idea applies directly to network vulnerability analysis, identifying single points of failure: ::: {#5401f701 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_edge("Client", "Gateway", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Gateway", "Server1", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Gateway", "Server2", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Server1", "Database", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Server2", "Database", auto_create_nodes=True) ) critical_nodes = graph.minimum_node_cut("Client", "Database") # Returns 1: Gateway is the single point of failure len(critical_nodes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: The same technique finds intermediaries in a social network: both must be removed to fully separate the two endpoints, since there are two independent paths between them: ::: {#852947b2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_edge("Alice", "Bob", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Bob", "Carol", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Alice", "Dave", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Dave", "Carol", auto_create_nodes=True) ) intermediaries = graph.minimum_node_cut("Alice", "Carol") # Returns both Bob's and Dave's node IDs len(intermediaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 2 ``` ::: :::
